query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: If Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs are subjected to systematically varied annealing temperatures and times after solution treatment, the resulting phase evolution (especially the formation of B2 and L12 phases) can be controlled, enabling property tuning.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs with a predominantly single-phase matrix.
generation.intervention: Post-solution annealing temperature and time variation (e.g., 700–1200°C for 1–10 hours).
generation.conditions: Inert atmosphere (e.g. argon), controlled cooling (quenching versus furnace cooling).
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitation and growth of ordered B2 and L12 phases within the FCC or BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature fosters diffusion-driven segregation and precipitation, which changes equilibrium phase fractions and stabilizes ordered domains.
generation.predicted_outcome: Observable changes in fraction and distribution of B2/L12 phases, leading to measurable differences in hardness and other mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: HEAs processed under identical conditions but without the systematic variation of annealing time/temperature (e.g., single-step annealing or no annealing).
generation.boundary: For annealing parameters outside the temperature or time range (e.g., below 700°C or above 1200°C, or very short/long times), phase evolution may differ or proceed incompletely, limiting control over microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: Exact phase fractions and transformation kinetics in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs remain partly uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose multiple alloy specimens to different annealing temperatures (700–1200°C) and dwell times (1–10 hours) after a common solution treatment, then compare resulting phases and microstructures using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy.
measurements: XRD patterns to quantify phase fractions
Electron microscopy to characterize microstructure and precipitate morphology
Hardness and tensile testing for mechanical property correlations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If B2/L12 phase fractions exhibit no systematic variation with changes in annealing schedule or if mechanical properties do not correlate with phase evolution, the hypothesis is falsified.
